**The brain is so boring**

If you thought tech bros were bad, wait until the brain bros arrive. [Werner Vogels’ predictions for 2027 and beyond](https://allthingsdistributed.com/2026/11/tech-predictions-for-2027-and-beyond.html) are out, and two of the five are about the brain: neurons on chips, and the mind becoming readable. Skin, gut and fascia get nothing. The nervous system gets a single mention, and that’s in a William Gibson reference.

People reliably think the brain is the most interesting thing in biology. I’d argue it’s the least. It’s the most over-studied organ in science and the most overwrought in culture: neuromarketing, neuroleadership, scans glowing on magazine covers. Brain bros love it because it’s simple. Not the wiring, the idea. Abstract, disembodied, a box of signals you can model, scan and plug things into. Nothing messy, nothing wet. Perhaps that’s why a certain class of people likes it so much.

The metaphor helps. Robert Epstein’s essay [The Empty Brain](https://aeon.co/essays/your-brain-does-not-process-information-and-it-is-not-a-computer) traced how every era describes the brain in terms of its own best technology. Just a few years after the dawn of computer technology in the 1940s, the brain was said to operate like a computer, and we’ve been stuck there ever since. The essay has been [thoroughly savaged](https://3quarksdaily.com/?p=223437), and some of the savaging is fair. But his central point holds. We keep treating the brain as hardware running software, and Vogels’ predictions are that conflation in its purest form: if the brain is a computer, then of course you can build one from neurons and read its outputs.

Evolution tells a different story. Peter Godfrey-Smith sets the familiar account of nervous systems, sense in and behaviour out, against an older and odder one: the first nervous systems came to exist as solutions to a problem of pure coordination within the organism. They were a way of getting a mass of cells to move as one body. He and his co-authors map out [both frameworks](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4650133), with the coordination view stressing the role of nervous systems in coordinating multicellular activity, especially muscle-based motility. The first version was probably [a nerve net, with specialised local circuits evolving later](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7935009). The body came first, and the brain arrived late to a party that was already going.

The octopus makes the point better than any argument. [More than half of its 500 million neurons are in its arms](https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2010/10/thinking-like-an-octopus), and the arms seem to have some autonomy of their own. Godfrey-Smith calls cephalopods [an entirely independent experiment](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/the-mind-of-an-octopus/) in large brains and complex behaviour, and what that experiment produced was a mind spread through a body.

Brain bros love a neuron count, as though intelligence were a matter of volume. But your gut is said to hold [more neurons than the entire spinal cord](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK11097/), and it gets on with its own reflexes without waiting for instructions from upstairs. It also has an ecosystem of its own. The skin is our largest sensing surface, the place where we meet the world. The nervous system runs through the whole body, not just the bit inside the skull. And the myofascial system is where thinking becomes biological sediment, settling into tissue over years of posture, habit and holding.

You’ll be thinking of [The Body Keeps the Score](https://www.besselvanderkolk.com/the-body-keeps-the-score.html). It did more than any book to make that idea mainstream, and it deserves credit for that. But its science has worn badly. One psychiatrist recently [worked through 122 of its claims](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/5DE000F0254747495B1CAFF4051C3B75/core-reader) on neurobiology, treatment and memory, and scientists have criticized the book for promoting pseudoscientific claims about trauma, memory, brains, and development. Ironically, much of the book is about the brain anyway. There are better places to start. Guy Claxton’s [Intelligence in the Flesh](https://yalebooks.yale.edu/book/9780300223477/intelligence-flesh/) argues that intelligence is not confined to the brain but is distributed throughout the body. Lisa Feldman Barrett, a neuroscientist, turns the whole thing round with [the theory that the brain evolved not to think but to control our bodies](https://www.apa.org/research/action/speaking-of-psychology/brain-myths). On her account, your brain keeps you alive and well by running a metabolic “budget” for your body. Even the brain’s biggest fans, read properly, end up pointing back at the body.

None of this can be seen at a single scale. There are cells and microbes at the micro level, tissues, fascial webs and organs at the meso, and a whole body moving through the world at the macro. The brain is one organ, studied mostly at one scale, while the interesting work happens across all three.

The brain is *so* boring. The rest of biology is where the fun is at.
